# FreshSave: Simulated Fresh Food Waste Dataset (4 Supermarkets, 2 Years)

**This dataset is SIMULATED.** It was generated by the script `make_store_dataset.py` (included). It is not data from real supermarkets.
Product types, shelf lives, demand levels, prices and seasons use typical retail values; every rule is written in the script.

## What one row is
One batch of fresh food on one evening of its shelf life (a daily snapshot). The question each row answers: **will this batch end with 20% or more of its units wasted?**

## Size
- 103,695 rows, 18 columns
- 25,656 batches, 4 stores, 8 categories, 40 product types (sub-categories)
- Dates: 2023-01-03 to 2025-01-12 (about two years)
- About 42% of batches are at risk. Total waste cost of all batches: $2,400,707
- 2% of `handling_score` values are missing on purpose (as in real data); everything else is complete

## Columns
| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| batch_id | Identifier of the delivered batch. Rows with the same batch_id are the same batch on different evenings |
| store_id | STORE_01 (large urban), STORE_02 (medium), STORE_03 (small town), STORE_04 (suburban) |
| date | Calendar date of the evening this row describes (YYYY-MM-DD). Data starts on Monday 2023-01-02 |
| category | Bakery, Beverages, Dairy, Deli, Meat, Produce, Ready_to_Eat, Seafood |
| sub_category | Product type, for example Whole Milk, Greek Yogurt, Salmon Fillet, Croissants |
| shelf_life_days | Total shelf life of the batch when it arrived (shorter than planned if the delivery was late) |
| days_left | Days left to sell on this evening (1 or more; the expiry evening itself is not a row) |
| units_received | Units delivered in the batch |
| units_left | Units counted on the shelf at the end of this evening (about 4% of counts have a small error) |
| avg_daily_demand | The product's normal units sold per day in that store |
| units_sold_today | Units sold on this day |
| cost_price | Cost per unit |
| selling_price | Selling price per unit (promoted batches are 15% cheaper) |
| handling_score | How well the batch was stored and moved, 1 (poor) to 10 (excellent). Sometimes missing |
| is_promoted | 1 if the batch was on promotion, else 0 |
| units_wasted_final | **Outcome.** Units left unsold at the end of the batch's life. Same value on every row of a batch |
| waste_cost | **Outcome.** units_wasted_final x cost_price |
| **at_risk** | **Target.** 1 if 20% or more of the batch was wasted, else 0 |

**Do not use `units_wasted_final`, `waste_cost` or `at_risk` as model inputs.** They are the result of the batch and would leak the answer. Use them for the target and for money reporting only.

## Split
Rows are in order of batch delivery (earlier batches first).
- `store_train_70.csv`: first 72,585 rows (70.0%), 17,919 batches (2023-01-03 to 2024-06-08), at risk 40.4% of rows
- `store_test_30.csv`: last 31,110 rows (30.0%), 7,737 batches (2024-05-27 to 2025-01-12), at risk 39.6% of rows
- `store_data_full.csv`: all rows together
No batch appears in both files. The split is by batch, so near the cut a few evenings of the last training batches fall on dates after the first test batches were delivered. If you split the data yourself, split by `batch_id` in time order, **not at random rows**, otherwise the same batch leaks into training and testing and scores look too good.

## How the data was simulated (summary)
Each store stocks its own range and delivers each product every few days. The manager orders about normal demand x planned shelf life, with ordering error. Each batch has its own demand level, unknown on delivery day; 5% of batches get a demand shock and 6% arrive late. Daily sales follow normal demand, the batch's demand level, a weekday effect (weekends sell more), a freshness effect (sales slow near expiry), a seasonal effect (drinks and salads sell more in summer) and random noise. Poor handling spoils a small share of the stock each day. Whatever is left at the end of the shelf life is waste. The share of at-risk batches was calibrated to about 42%. It was not tuned to any model's accuracy.

## Suggested uses
Classification (will a batch be wasted?), model comparison (KNN, Decision Tree and others), store and category comparison, waste-cost reporting, feature engineering, for example `units_received - units_left` (sold so far) and `units_left / avg_daily_demand - days_left` (stock cover versus days left).

## Limits
- Simulated data: scores on it show a method works, not how it would perform in a real store.
- Only 4 stores and about two years, so seasonal patterns are limited to what the simulator contains.
